newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - Compulsory insurance for ship.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - Compulsory insurance for ship.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
Marine insurers hoping the issue of compulsory ships'
insurance will go away because it is too difficult for the International Maritime Organisation (IMO)to implement may have to think again.

The European Commission yesterday signalled its determination to run with the issue itself if the IMO does not come up with proposals it regards as adequate at the marine organisation's Legal Committee meeting in April.
At the heart of the Commission's interest in compulsory third party insurance for all ships entering European ports, is its desire to rid Europe's waters of substandard shipping.

The Commission has made clear its preference for an international agreement is international, but Maritime Safety and Pollution Prevention unit official Stefan Lindstrom has warned that non-binding IMO resolutions will not be acceptable. He insisted that attempts to carry on "business as usual" will not be tolerated.

Besides which unilateral action from countries such as the UK, which is preparing to enforce compulsory insurance on ships entering its ports in the Merchant Shipping and Maritime Security Bill, will add pressure to the drive for a common approach.

The Commission says it wants dialogue with the marine insurance industry. It wants feedback in order to ensure a workable system which succeeds in bolstering its ultimate aim of banning substandard shipping and ensuring standard passengers' rights to compensation across Europe.
And the marine insurance industry has a vested interest in taking part in the Commission's deliberations, for there are a number of contentious issues which need to be settled.
Not least is whether liability should reside with the operator of the ship or its registered shipowner.

Uniform liabilities would need to be set, as well as standards required for obtaining insurance and those applied by port state inspectors. The cost of administering a compulsory insurance regime has also been raised.

Advances to information technology have recently allowed it for the first time to ban a ship from entering its ports after changes to its ownership, class and flag meant that UK-required port state repairs were evaded.
The same electronic tracking and notification systems are being used to check a sample of 200 detained ships to evaluate their insurers and classification socities.
There can be little doubt that having gone so far down the road to regulating shipping safety standards, the EC will insist on taking action on insurance.
